questions.q: How does this lesson characterize Salesforce's 'declarative-first' guidance?
options: A rigid law that forbids writing Apex under any circumstances
A starting point for judgment -- default to declarative tools, reach for code once a requirement genuinely outgrows them -- not a rule that overrides evaluating the actual requirement
A marketing term with no real influence on architecture decisions
A rule that applies only to Flow, never to validation rules or approval processes
questions.explain: The lesson frames declarative-first as sound default guidance, but warns against reflexively applying it as a slogan once a requirement has clearly outgrown declarative tools -- the actual factors should decide, not the slogan.

questions.q: Which of these is correctly listed in this lesson as a real Apex governor limit?
options: A single Apex transaction can issue at most 100 SOQL queries synchronously (200 asynchronously)
A single Apex transaction can issue an unlimited number of SOQL queries as long as it runs asynchronously
A single Apex transaction can process at most 100 records via DML operations
Governor limits only apply to Flow, never to Apex
questions.explain: The documented synchronous/asynchronous SOQL query limits are 100 and 200 respectively; DML record processing is capped at 10,000 records per transaction, not 100, and governor limits apply specifically to Apex execution.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why do governor limits exist at all?
options: To make Apex intentionally harder to learn than Flow
Because the platform is multi-tenant, and no single customer's code can be allowed to consume unbounded shared resources
They exist only in sandbox orgs, not in production
They exist solely to generate error messages for test classes
questions.explain: Governor limits are a direct consequence of Salesforce's shared, multi-tenant infrastructure -- they prevent one customer's code from degrading the platform for every other tenant sharing the same resources.

questions.q: Which of the following is named in this lesson as a case where Apex has capability Flow doesn't match?
options: Running simple field-update automation on record save
Asynchronous and scheduled processing patterns like Batch Apex, Queueable Apex, and Scheduled Apex
Displaying a related list on a Lightning record page
Enforcing field-level security on a custom object
questions.explain: The lesson specifically names Batch Apex, Queueable Apex, and Scheduled Apex as asynchronous/scheduled patterns with no equivalent fidelity in pure declarative tooling.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue the declarative-vs-programmatic decision is not a one-time, permanent choice?
options: Because Salesforce forces a re-evaluation of every Flow every year automatically

Because a solution built declaratively when requirements were simple can legitimately need to move to Apex once requirements grow in complexity or volume -- treating the choice as permanent is itself an architecture mistake
Because Flow and Apex produce identical results in every case, so the choice never actually matters
Because governor limits change every release, making any earlier decision obsolete automatically
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues that requirements evolve -- a Flow built for a simple case can be outgrown by new complexity or scale, and the decision should be revisited rather than fixed at project kickoff.
